finding.claim: reset_password_loose uses loose == to compare the stored reset token with the caller-supplied $token, so a boolean true (e.g. from JSON input) matches any stored token and the password is changed. High if reachable with JSON input; otherwise low.
finding.source: $token argument, untyped; boolean true or other type-juggling value supplied by the caller

trace.note: Fetch stored token for $email from resets table
Loose comparison $row['token'] == $token; non-empty string == true is true on all PHP versions

finding.guards_checked: $db->quote() on email (no SQLi); password_hash on new password. No type check on $token, no hash_equals, no expiry or attempt limit in this function.

verdict.guard_found: none. reset.php:4 is a bare `==` with no type check, hash_equals, or expiry/attempt limit. The only other condition is that a reset row exists for $email (reset.php:3), which is a precondition, not a guard. reset_password (reset.php:12-14) uses hash_equals, but no caller of either function is in the directory.
verdict.reason: The type-juggling flaw is real: reset.php:4 `$row['token'] == $token` is true when $token is boolean true and the stored token is a non-empty string, and the trace at reset.php:3-5 matches the code. Whether an anonymous attacker can reach it is undecidable here, because no caller of reset_password_loose exists in this directory, so the JSON-input reachability that determines severity cannot be confirmed.

finding.claim: Reset tokens are never consumed or expired and are stored and compared in plaintext. A valid token can be replayed indefinitely, and concurrent requests can both succeed (TOCTOU). High.
finding.source: Any holder of a previously issued reset token for an email

trace.note: Raw token selected from resets for $email
Password updated; the resets row is not deleted or marked used
Separate SELECT and UPDATE with no transaction, so concurrent requests with the same token can both succeed

finding.guards_checked: hash_equals is timing-safe. No expiry column, single-use marker, or transaction referenced anywhere in the code.

verdict.guard_found: none. reset.php:13-14 compares the raw stored token with hash_equals, which is timing-safe but is not an expiry, single-use, or ownership control. reset.php:15-17 updates the password and returns without deleting or marking the resets row. The only other file in the directory is a skill doc, so nothing in the repo deletes or expires the row.
verdict.reason: At reset.php:13-17 the token is selected in plaintext, checked with hash_equals, and never invalidated, so any previously issued token for that email can reset the password again indefinitely. The attacker must already hold an old token, which is a real but narrower precondition than "anyone", and the TOCTOU point at reset.php:13-16 adds nothing because replay already succeeds without a race. The caller and route that expose reset_password are not in this directory, so exposure is unverified, but the flaw itself is confirmed.

finding.claim: The strict reset_password accepts an empty or NULL stored token when the caller passes null, false or empty string, because (string) casts them to '' and PHP coerces a NULL stored value to '' in hash_equals. Medium, conditional on rows with NULL or empty tokens existing.
finding.source: $token set to null, false or '' by the caller; NULL or '' token stored in resets

trace.note: Stored token fetched for $email; may be NULL or ''
(string)$token yields ''; hash_equals(NULL or '', '') returns true (NULL coerced to '' with a deprecation notice on PHP 8.1+)

finding.guards_checked: hash_equals and the (string) cast are present but do not reject empty values. No check that the stored token is non-empty.

verdict.guard_found: none. reset.php:14 has only `$row &&` and hash_equals; nothing rejects an empty or NULL stored token, and the return value is used directly for the update at reset.php:15-16.
verdict.reason: The trace is accurate: at reset.php:14, `(string)$token` turns null/false into '' and hash_equals against a NULL or '' stored token returns true, so the UPDATE at reset.php:15-16 runs with no effective guard. But whether any resets row has a NULL or empty token is not determinable from this directory, which holds only reset.php and no schema, data, or caller code, so exploitability depends on data state that cannot be verified here.

finding.claim: No validation of the new password: empty passwords are accepted and bcrypt (PASSWORD_DEFAULT) silently truncates input beyond 72 bytes. Low.

trace.note: $new passed directly to password_hash(..., PASSWORD_DEFAULT) with no length or emptiness check
Hash stored in users.pw; bytes past 72 are ignored under bcrypt

finding.guards_checked: No validation of $new in this file. Password policy may be enforced by the caller, which is not visible in this directory.

verdict.guard_found: None in reset.php. The only gate is the token check at reset.php:4 (loose ==) and reset.php:14 (hash_equals) before the update at lines 5-6 and 15-16. The candidate's trace lines exist and match: $new goes straight into password_hash with no length or emptiness check. Line 6 is the continuation of the same UPDATE statement that starts at line 5.
verdict.reason: The write at reset.php:5-6 (and 15-16) is reachable only by someone who already holds a valid reset token (reset.php:14), and that holder can already set any password they choose, so accepting an empty or long password grants no new power. Bcrypt truncation past 72 bytes only weakens the password the account owner picks, which is a password-policy hygiene issue, not an authentication bypass or vulnerability. Whether the caller enforces a password policy is not visible here, and it does not change the outcome. Separately, reset.php:4 uses loose == for the token comparison; that is a different issue and not part of this candidate.

finding.claim: The UPDATE affected-row count is never checked, so the function returns true even when no users row matches $email. Low / informational; can mislead callers and enable account-existence probing if the return value is exposed.
finding.source: $email argument with no matching users row but a resets row present
finding.sink: Return value true from reset_password_loose (reset.php:7) and reset_password (reset.php:17)

trace.note: UPDATE users ... WHERE email = ... executed without checking rowCount()
Function returns true regardless of rows updated

finding.guards_checked: None. Callers' handling of the return value is not visible in this directory.

verdict.guard_found: none. reset.php:5-6 runs the UPDATE as a bare exec() statement with no rowCount() check, and reset.php:7 returns true unconditionally after it. Within this directory, no caller inspects the return value. The only check is the token match at reset.php:4 (loose) and reset.php:14 (strict, hash_equals), and that check is on the resets row, not on the users row.
verdict.reason: The mechanical defect is real: reset.php:5-7 returns true after an UPDATE that may match zero users rows, since no rowCount() check exists. The account-existence probing impact is not supported, because the true/false result at reset.php:4 and reset.php:14 depends on token match against the resets table, not on whether a users row exists, so the attacker must already hold a valid token. Severity should stay low.
